questions.stem: A 14-month-old with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot becomes deeply cyanotic, irritable and breathes rapidly and deeply after crying through a blood draw. The SpO2 falls from 82% to 64%. The parent is holding the child. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Have the parent hold the child with knees drawn to the chest
Lay the child flat on the bed and apply oxygen by face mask
Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus through the IV
Prepare to give IV morphine as prescribed to calm the child's breathing

rationale.correct: Hypercyanotic ('tet') spell: knee-chest, calm the child, oxygen, then morphine and fluids as ordered.

perOption.a: Knee-chest positioning raises systemic resistance and pushes more blood through the lungs.
perOption.b: Oxygen helps, but lying flat does not reduce the right-to-left shunt; positioning comes first.
perOption.c: Fluids may be ordered after positioning.
perOption.d: Morphine may be given if positioning and calming fail.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a teaching session for parents of children on the pediatric cardiac unit, using a diagram of blood flow through the heart. For each congenital heart defect, indicate whether it increases pulmonary blood flow, decreases pulmonary blood flow or obstructs blood flow.

rationale.correct: Classify congenital heart defects by how they change blood flow.

perOption.r1:c1: A left-to-right shunt increases blood flow to the lungs.
perOption.r1:c2: VSD is not cyanotic in its usual form.
perOption.r1:c3: VSD is not an obstructive lesion.
perOption.r2:c2: Pulmonary stenosis with a right-to-left shunt causes cyanosis.
perOption.r2:c3: Its main feature is reduced pulmonary flow.
perOption.r3:c1: This is not a shunt lesion.
perOption.r4:c1: A left-to-right shunt increases blood flow to the lungs.
perOption.r5:c1: Blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery, increasing lung flow.
perOption.r6:c1: This is not a shunt lesion.
perOption.r6:c3: A narrowed aortic valve obstructs flow out of the left ventricle.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old is brought in for poor feeding and fussiness. The infant is pink, the heart rate is 168/min and a soft murmur is heard. Which additional finding most suggests coarctation of the aorta?

options.text: Arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg higher than in the legs
Bounding pulses that are equal in the four extremities
Oxygen saturation of 78% in the right hand and foot
A barking cough and inspiratory stridor

rationale.correct: Coarctation: compare blood pressures in the arms and legs and check the femoral pulses.

perOption.a: The narrowing limits blood flow to the lower body.
perOption.b: Femoral pulses are weak or absent in coarctation.
perOption.c: Coarctation is usually acyanotic.
perOption.d: These suggest an airway problem.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with a large ventricular septal defect is seen for a weight check. The parent says feedings take 45 minutes and the baby sweats on the head while feeding. Which other finding would the nurse expect if heart failure is developing?

options.text: Breathing at 68/min and a liver edge 3 cm below the ribs
Weight gain of 40 g per day since the visit 4 weeks ago
A respiratory rate of 24/min with easy breathing
Increased activity and alertness for an hour after feedings

rationale.correct: Infant heart failure: feeding problems, diaphoresis, tachypnea, poor growth and hepatomegaly.

perOption.a: Tachypnea and hepatomegaly are classic signs of infant heart failure.
perOption.b: Infants in heart failure gain weight poorly.
perOption.c: Tachypnea is typical.
perOption.d: Fatigue after feedings is typical.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with heart failure is prescribed digoxin 0.03 mg orally twice daily. Before the 0900 dose, the nurse counts an apical pulse of 84/min for 1 full minute. The infant vomited twice this morning. The last digoxin level was 1.4 ng/mL a week ago. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider
Give the dose, since the last level was in range
Give half the dose and recheck the pulse in 1 hour
Recheck the pulse in 4 hours and give the dose then

rationale.correct: Pediatric digoxin: count the apical pulse for 1 full minute and hold per the parameters (infants below about 90 to 110; children below about 70). Vomiting and bradycardia suggest toxicity.

perOption.a: An infant's digoxin is usually held for a heart rate below about 90 to 110; bradycardia with vomiting suggests toxicity.
perOption.b: The heart rate is too low, and the vomiting may be a sign of toxicity.
perOption.c: The nurse cannot change the dose.
perOption.d: The provider needs to know about the bradycardia and vomiting now.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with Kawasaki disease received IV immune globulin yesterday and is now on low-dose aspirin. The fever has resolved. The child is due for the MMR and varicella vaccines next month. Which discharge teaching is accurate?

options.text: Postpone the MMR and varicella vaccines for about 11 months
Stop the aspirin now that the fever has gone away
Give ibuprofen with the aspirin for joint pain or fever
The heart is safe now, so follow-up echocardiograms are not needed

rationale.correct: Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 days or more, red eyes, strawberry tongue, peeling hands; risk of coronary aneurysm; IVIG and aspirin.

perOption.a: Antibodies in IVIG can block the immune response to live vaccines.
perOption.b: Low-dose aspirin often continues for 6 to 8 weeks as directed.
perOption.c: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin's antiplatelet effect.
perOption.d: Coronary artery aneurysms can develop over weeks and need follow-up.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 4-week-old first-born infant has vomited forcefully across the room after most feeds for 3 days, then seems hungry right away. The vomit contains formula but no bile. The nurse feels a small, firm mass in the upper right abdomen. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Pyloric stenosis
Intussusception
Gastroesophageal reflux
Malrotation with volvulus

rationale.correct: Pyloric stenosis: projectile vomiting, hunger, olive mass and metabolic alkalosis.

perOption.a: A thickened pylorus causes projectile, non-bilious vomiting and a palpable olive.
perOption.b: This causes colicky pain and currant jelly stools.
perOption.c: Reflux causes effortless spitting up, not projectile vomiting with a mass.
perOption.d: This causes bilious vomiting.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old has had episodes of screaming with the knees drawn up every 15 to 20 minutes, with quiet periods between. The infant has vomited twice and just passed a stool of blood and mucus. The nurse feels a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Intussusception
Pyloric stenosis
Infant colic
Bacterial gastroenteritis

rationale.correct: Intussusception: sudden colicky pain, a sausage-shaped mass and currant jelly stools. Report a normal brown stool, which may mean it has reduced.

perOption.a: Telescoping bowel causes colicky pain, a sausage-shaped mass and currant jelly stools.
perOption.b: This affects younger infants and causes projectile vomiting without bloody stool.
perOption.c: Colic does not cause bloody stools or a mass.
perOption.d: This causes diarrhea and fever but not a sausage-shaped mass.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A term newborn has not passed meconium at 48 hours of age. The abdomen is distended, the infant has started vomiting green fluid and a rectal exam is followed by an explosive release of stool. Which condition do these findings suggest?

options.text: Hirschsprung disease
Pyloric stenosis
Meconium aspiration
Intussusception

rationale.correct: Hirschsprung disease: delayed meconium, distension, bilious vomiting and later ribbon-like, foul-smelling stools.

perOption.a: Missing nerve cells in part of the bowel prevent stool from passing; a rectal exam can release a burst of stool.
perOption.b: This causes non-bilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks.
perOption.c: This affects the lungs, not stool passage.
perOption.d: This is unusual in newborns.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old has had diarrhea for 2 days. The parent says the baby is "not acting right." Which group of findings suggests the infant is dehydrated?

options.text: Sunken fontanel and 2 wet diapers in 24 hours
Bulging anterior fontanel and a high-pitched cry
Moist mucous membranes and tears when crying
Weight up 100 g from last week's visit

rationale.correct: Infant dehydration: sunken fontanel and eyes, dry membranes, fewer wet diapers, tachycardia and lethargy.

perOption.a: These are signs of volume loss.
perOption.b: These suggest increased intracranial pressure.
perOption.c: These show good hydration.
perOption.d: Weight loss, not gain, suggests dehydration.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with gastroenteritis has vomited 3 times and had 5 loose stools today. The child is alert, has moist lips and is drinking. Mild dehydration is diagnosed. What should the nurse teach the parents?

options.text: Give 5 mL of oral rehydration solution every few minutes
Give large cups of apple juice or a sports drink
Withhold food and fluids for 24 hours to rest the gut
Give plain water and hold solid foods for the next several days

rationale.correct: Mild to moderate dehydration: ORS in small frequent amounts, then resume a normal diet.

perOption.a: Small, frequent amounts of ORS replace fluid and electrolytes and are tolerated even with vomiting.
perOption.b: High sugar can worsen diarrhea and lacks the right electrolytes.
perOption.c: This worsens dehydration.
perOption.d: Water lacks electrolytes, and a normal diet resumes once rehydrated.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old returns from surgery after a cleft lip repair. The infant is fussy, rubbing the face against the sheet and trying to suck the fingers. Which action should the nurse take to protect the repair?

options.text: Place the infant on the back and apply elbow restraints
Place the infant prone so secretions can drain from the mouth
Give a pacifier to soothe the infant and stop the crying
Swaddle the infant face down on the parent's chest

rationale.correct: Cleft lip repair: protect the suture line, no prone positioning, elbow restraints and gentle cleaning.

perOption.a: Lying supine keeps the lip off the sheet, and elbow restraints keep the hands away from the suture line.
perOption.b: Prone positioning rubs the lip against the bed.
perOption.c: Sucking strains the suture line.
perOption.d: This presses the repair against the parent.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old wakes at night scratching around the anus, and the provider suspects pinworms. The nurse is teaching the parent how to collect a tape test at home. When should the parent collect the sample?

options.text: First thing in the morning, before bathing or using the toilet
At bedtime, after the child has been bathed and dressed for sleep
After the morning bath, once the skin is clean and dry
Within an hour after the child eats breakfast

rationale.correct: Pinworms: morning tape test, treat the whole family, wash bedding and use good hand hygiene.

perOption.a: Female worms lay eggs around the anus at night.
perOption.b: Eggs are laid overnight, so morning collection finds them.
perOption.c: Bathing removes the eggs.
perOption.d: Timing relates to egg-laying, not meals.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has swelling around the eyes in the morning, a swollen abdomen and frothy urine. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Urine protein is 4+ with no blood, serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and cholesterol is 320 mg/dL. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Nephrotic syndrome
Acute glomerulonephritis
Urinary tract infection
Wilms tumor

rationale.correct: Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia; treated with corticosteroids.

perOption.a: Massive protein loss causes low albumin, edema and high cholesterol.
perOption.b: This causes hematuria and hypertension.
perOption.c: This does not cause massive proteinuria or edema.
perOption.d: This causes a firm abdominal mass, not generalized edema.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted after a parent noticed a firm, smooth mass on one side of the abdomen while bathing the child. A Wilms tumor is suspected, and surgery is planned for tomorrow. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Post a sign at the bedside that says not to palpate the abdomen
Measure the mass by palpation each shift to track its growth
Take blood pressures in the thigh to avoid disturbing the child
Give a soapsuds enema to empty the bowel before surgery

rationale.correct: Wilms tumor: post a sign to avoid abdominal palpation and handle the child carefully.

perOption.a: Palpation can rupture the tumor capsule and spread cancer cells.
perOption.b: Palpation risks rupturing the tumor.
perOption.c: Blood pressure is checked in the arm; Wilms tumor can cause hypertension.
perOption.d: This is not routine and could disturb the tumor.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect a child with a Wilms tumor.

questions.stem: A newborn boy has hypospadias with the urethral opening on the underside of the penis. The parents planned a circumcision before discharge and ask the nurse whether it can still be done. What should the nurse tell the parents?

options.text: "It is delayed; the foreskin may be needed for the repair."
"Circumcision should be done now so the area heals before the repair."
"No repair is needed, because this does not affect urination."
"The repair is done at puberty, once growth is complete."

rationale.correct: Hypospadias: no circumcision; surgical repair is usually done between 6 and 12 months.

perOption.a: The foreskin may be used as tissue during surgical repair.
perOption.b: Removing the foreskin may prevent a good repair.
perOption.c: Surgery is usually done in infancy to correct the stream and appearance.
perOption.d: Repair is usually done between 6 and 12 months.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure at home with a temperature of 39.4 °C (103 °F) and is now alert and playful. The provider diagnoses a simple febrile seizure. The parent asks what to do if it happens again. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Turn the child on the side; call 911 if it lasts over 5 minutes
Put a soft object between the child's teeth to protect the tongue
Put the child in a cool bath to bring the fever down quickly
Give acetaminophen around the clock to prevent seizures

rationale.correct: Simple febrile seizures are usually benign; teach seizure first aid.

perOption.a: Most febrile seizures are brief; protecting the airway and timing the seizure are key.
perOption.b: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or block the airway.
perOption.c: A cool bath during a seizure risks drowning and is not recommended.
perOption.d: Antipyretics are for comfort and do not prevent febrile seizures.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At a 4-month well-baby visit, the infant's head circumference has moved from the 50th to above the 95th percentile since the 2-month visit. The parent says the baby is more irritable and feeds poorly. Which other findings would most suggest hydrocephalus?

options.text: A bulging fontanel and eyes that look downward
A sunken fontanel and dry mucous membranes
A closed anterior fontanel and a small forehead
Flattening on one side of the back of the head

rationale.correct: Hydrocephalus in infants: increasing head circumference, bulging fontanel, sunset eyes and irritability.

perOption.a: These show CSF building up and pressing on the brain.
perOption.b: These suggest dehydration.
perOption.c: Early closure fits craniosynostosis or microcephaly.
perOption.d: This is positional plagiocephaly.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt has vomited 4 times since this morning and has a headache and is sleepier than usual. The sibling has a stomach virus. The temperature is 37.2 °C (99 °F), the pulse is 64/min and the blood pressure is 128/62 mm Hg. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Shunt malfunction with increased intracranial pressure
Viral gastroenteritis caught from the sibling at home
Shunt infection spreading along the tubing to the abdomen
Dehydration from repeated vomiting

rationale.correct: Shunt malfunction: signs of increased ICP. Shunt infection: fever and redness along the tract.

perOption.a: Vomiting, headache and drowsiness with bradycardia and a widening pulse pressure suggest rising ICP.
perOption.b: This is possible, but the vital signs point to rising ICP, which must be ruled out first.
perOption.c: Infection usually causes fever and redness along the tract.
perOption.d: Dehydration causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A term newborn is born with a myelomeningocele in the lumbar area. The sac is intact, and surgery is planned within 48 hours. How should the nurse care for the sac until surgery?

options.text: Cover with a sterile, saline-moist nonadherent dressing; position prone
Leave it open to air under the radiant warmer so it can be watched closely
Place the newborn on the back with a rolled towel under the hips
Cover it with dry sterile gauze secured with tape

rationale.correct: Myelomeningocele: sterile moist dressing, prone position, latex precautions and watch for hydrocephalus.

perOption.a: This keeps the sac moist and free of pressure and lowers the risk of rupture and infection.
perOption.b: Drying can crack the sac and allow infection.
perOption.c: This puts pressure on the sac.
perOption.d: Dry gauze sticks to the sac and can tear it.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old born at 28 weeks is seen for a developmental check. The parent says the baby feels "stiff" when picked up. Which finding is an early sign of cerebral palsy?

options.text: A Moro reflex still present, with legs that scissor
Rolling over from front to back and from back to front
Babbling with consonant sounds such as "ba-ba"
Passing a toy from one hand to the other

rationale.correct: CP: persistent primitive reflexes, abnormal tone, delayed milestones and early hand preference.

perOption.a: Persistent primitive reflexes and increased tone suggest CP.
perOption.b: This is expected at this age.
perOption.c: This is expected.
perOption.d: This is expected.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old is brought in with a temperature of 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), poor feeding and vomiting for 12 hours. The infant has no neck stiffness. Which additional finding most strongly suggests bacterial meningitis?

options.text: A bulging fontanel with a high-pitched cry
Clear nasal discharge and a mild cough
A sunken fontanel and few wet diapers
Red, bulging eardrum on otoscope exam

rationale.correct: Infant meningitis may lack neck stiffness; look for a bulging fontanel, irritability, poor feeding and a high-pitched cry.

perOption.a: These suggest increased ICP and meningeal irritation; infants often lack neck stiffness.
perOption.b: This suggests a viral upper respiratory infection.
perOption.c: This suggests dehydration from vomiting.
perOption.d: This suggests otitis media, a common cause of fever.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A parent calls the clinic about a 9-year-old with influenza who has a fever of 39 °C (102.2 °F) and body aches. The parent asks whether the child can take aspirin from the family medicine cabinet. What is the best response?

options.text: "No, aspirin can cause Reye syndrome; use acetaminophen or ibuprofen."
"Yes, aspirin works best for fever and the aches of the flu."
"Yes, but give half of an adult tablet to lower the risk."
"Yes, as long as you give it with food or milk to protect the stomach."

rationale.correct: Avoid aspirin in children and teens with viral illnesses (influenza, varicella).

perOption.a: Aspirin during a viral illness can cause Reye syndrome (liver failure and brain swelling).
perOption.b: Aspirin is avoided in children with viral illness.
perOption.c: Any amount carries the risk.
perOption.d: Food does not prevent Reye syndrome.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
